Lesson 5 · Anticipate next week

How should we compare different stores?

The simple line connects longer delivery times with greater stockout pressure. The director now asks for comparisons that reflect the different environments in which stores operate.

Baseline profiles · weeks 1–8 · the same 150 stores

Method in this decision: Multiple regression and interactions

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The decision brief

An urban store running frequent promotions may face a different workload from another store with the same delivery cycle. We will extend the existing regression to include location, demand, and promotion exposure, then allow the delivery-time slope to differ by location. The output is a set of specified store profiles that operations can use for planning. We keep the same rows and outcome as Lesson 4.

Ask how precisely the fitted relationships are known

A coefficient estimate comes with sampling uncertainty

Multiple-regression coefficient report
TermEstimateRobust SE95% interval
Intercept5.340.484.39 to 6.29
Lead days1.530.121.29 to 1.77
Urban1.000.60-0.18 to 2.18
Demand above 1000.060.010.04 to 0.07
Promotion share2.940.491.99 to 3.90
Lead × urban0.230.16-0.09 to 0.54

The coefficients describe the specified model for the store population represented by the baseline. Robust standard errors allow the residual variance to differ across stores. For a single coefficient, a large-sample interval is estimate ±1.96×SE, and a zero-slope test compares the estimate with zero in standard-error units. Keep 95% intervals paired with two-sided 5% tests.

The mean prediction and a new store are different targets

Simple-model interval demonstration
Lead daysFitted mean95% mean interval95% individual interval
210.209.74 to 10.656.97 to 13.42
3.512.6212.36 to 12.889.42 to 15.83

A confidence interval concerns the average outcome at the specified delivery time. An individual prediction interval adds the variation of a new store around that mean, so it is wider. This teaching calculation uses the simple model with constant residual variance; the coefficient table above uses robust uncertainty for the richer model.

State which store characteristics enter the comparison

The outcome remains the eight-week baseline rate. Inputs are delivery days, urban location, average observed baseline demand, and the share of baseline weeks with a promotion. These observed baseline variables help explain the baseline comparison. The timing needed for a future forecast will be handled explicitly in Lesson 6.

The urban flag equals one for urban stores and zero otherwise. Demand is centered at 100, so a value of zero in the regression means demand at the reference level. Promotion share ranges from zero to one. A value of 0.25 means promotion in a quarter of the observed weeks.

Let a comparison change with location

Predicted rate = b0 + b1 × lead + b2 × urban + b3 × (demand − 100) + b4 × promotion share + b5 × lead × urban

The extended baseline model
TermFitted coefficient
Intercept5.34
Lead days1.53
Urban1.00
Demand above 1000.06
Promotion share2.94
Lead × urban0.23

The product lead × urban is the interaction. For a nonurban store, urban is zero and the product vanishes. Its delivery slope is b1. For an urban store, the product adds b5 to that slope. This is how the equation represents a relationship that differs by store type.

Nonurban delivery slope: 1.53 points/day. Urban delivery slope: 1.76 points/day.

To calculate a profile, specify all inputs and substitute them into the same equation. That is more informative than selecting one coefficient and calling it the answer for every store.

Explain why adding a variable changes a coefficient

Omitted-variable bias has two ingredients

Short-model slope = long-model slope + omitted-variable effect × sorting slope

An omitted factor can change a fitted slope when it is associated with both the included predictor and the outcome. The sorting slope comes from regressing the omitted factor on the included predictor. This algebra describes a change between regressions; a causal interpretation additionally depends on the business assignment process.

Check the identity on the retail stores

Adding urban location to the simple regression
ComponentValue
Lead slope without location1.62
Lead slope with location1.68
Location coefficient × lead–location sorting-0.07

1.62 = 1.68 + -0.07

The auxiliary regression uses urban location as its dependent variable and delivery time as its predictor. The product’s sign tells us which way the short-model slope shifts. These are deliberately nested models on the same 150 stores, so a sample change cannot explain the difference.

Categories need a reference group

  • With K categories and an intercept, include K−1 indicators.
  • Name the omitted reference category.
  • Interpret each coefficient relative to that category.
  • Keep coding rules aligned when predicting new rows.

For delivery categories 2, 3, 4, and 5 days, choose two days as the reference and create three indicators. A label such as urban=1 needs a documented meaning. Including every indicator with an intercept creates redundant columns rather than additional information.

An interaction makes a slope depend on context

Rate = a + b × lead + c × urban + d × lead × urban

The lead-time slope is b for nonurban stores and b+d for urban stores. The urban difference at a particular delivery time is c+d×lead. For two continuous predictors, an interaction similarly lets the marginal association of one depend on the level of the other. Centring a predictor can make the reference point more useful.

Read fit and residuals together

  • Training R²: 0.82
  • Adjusted R²: 0.82
  • Inspect actual-versus-fitted values and residuals

Adjusted R² accounts for the number of fitted parameters when summarizing training fit. Neither statistic substitutes for new-data evaluation. In an actual-versus-fitted plot, state which variable is on which axis: with fitted on the horizontal axis, points above the diagonal have actual rates higher than predicted.

Read predictions for a common operating scenario

These profiles keep demand and promotion exposure fixed while changing delivery time and location. They make the comparison concrete: a manager can identify which row resembles a store in the operating plan and see which other inputs were held constant.

The simple slope in Lesson 4 was 1.62 points per day. The extended model answers a more specific question by accounting for the measured store mix and allowing different slopes. Its baseline RMSE is 1.00 points, calculated on the same 150 profiles.

An urban-location coefficient by itself refers to the difference when lead is zero in this specification. That is outside the observed delivery range. Reading complete profiles avoids giving that isolated coefficient an unintended operating interpretation.

A residual shortlist asks a useful operational question: what is happening here that the recorded profile does not explain? Ask about delivery disruptions, local practices, and measurement. The model makes the comparison more specific; the next conversation supplies information the columns do not contain.

Turn a coefficient into a sentence

  • How should the director interpret an interaction?
Discuss, then reveal

Name two store profiles, hold their other inputs fixed, calculate both fitted outcomes, and report the difference in percentage points. This is clearer than presenting the interaction coefficient without the main effects or the comparison level.

How would you explain the interaction result to a director who needs a store comparison?

Carry the comparison into forecast design

Use the profile table to discuss where a fixed amount of operational attention may be insufficient. Ask whether the variables correspond to information managers recognize and whether the combinations reflect stores the chain actually operates.

The comparison also suggests useful forecast inputs: location and usual delivery time are known in advance; planned promotions and a demand forecast can be prepared before next week. The next lesson tests that forecasting procedure on later weeks instead of evaluating it on the rows used to fit it.

Update the decision memo

Compare specified store profiles. Delivery-time slopes are 1.53 points per day for nonurban stores and 1.76 for urban stores in the extended baseline model. Use these relationships to design a forecast and operating review.

Make the call

Why does the urban delivery slope include two coefficients?

Compare your reasoning

For urban=1, both lead and lead×urban change when lead changes. Their coefficients add. For urban=0, the interaction is zero.

The bigger picture

The value of a richer model is a more useful comparison. Keeping the outcome, population, and input values explicit lets a manager see which differences the model accounts for and which scenario a prediction represents.

After your decision: open the known answer

The shared baseline mechanism contains an interaction between delivery time and urban location. The fitted profiles recover an estimate of that pattern from the same store records used for the simple regression.
